title: Silver Galactic Sliver
caption: The Silver Sliver Galaxy, NGC 891, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA Acknowledgments: PI: M.T. Patterson (New Mexico State University). Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Mahdi Zamani & Davide de Martin

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A spiral galaxy seen almost perfectly edge-on stretches across this image as a long, thin sliver. This is NGC 891, nicknamed the Silver Sliver Galaxy, captured with the Mosaic instrument on the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory. Viewed this way, it bears a striking resemblance to our own Milky Way as we see it from Earth.

Its edge-on angle makes NGC 891 a good place to test the galactic fountain model. In this picture, stellar winds and supernovae in a galaxy's disk blast gas out into the surrounding space. Some of that gas can condense and rain back down onto the disk, where it becomes fresh fuel for new stars. Seeing a disk side-on makes gas above and below it easier to spot.

The frame is also crowded with other objects near and far. Bright foreground stars in our own galaxy intrude on the view, while distant galaxies lurk in the background. NGC 891 lies in the direction of the constellation Andromeda.

understand.summary: Taken with the Mosaic camera on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope through U, B, R and hydrogen-alpha filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
